subject: chemistry
title: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.6.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium, specification section 4.6.2.
final_note: You worked through Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium — 25 specification statements.

concepts.def: A reaction in which the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. The change is not a dead end: once some product has formed, that product is able to turn back into the starting substances.

The double half-arrow used to represent a reversible reaction, as in A + B ⇌ C + D. It shows that A and B can react to give C and D, and that C and D can react to give A and B. A single arrow → would mean only one of those two changes is possible.

In A + B ⇌ C + D the forward reaction is A + B → C + D, read left to right, and the reverse reaction is C + D → A + B, read right to left. Which substances count as 'reactants' therefore depends on which of the two reactions is being described.

concepts.term: Changing the direction by changing the conditions
concepts.def: The direction of a reversible reaction can be changed by changing the conditions. The same set of substances can be made to go one way under one set of conditions, such as heating, and the other way under another, such as cooling.

concepts.term: Ammonium chloride: a worked example of changing direction
concepts.def: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride, or NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. Heating the white solid drives the forward reaction and produces the two gases; where the gases meet a cooler surface the reverse reaction happens and white solid ammonium chloride forms again.

concepts.term: Energy transfer in the two directions
concepts.def: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each case. If the forward reaction transfers a given quantity of energy to the surroundings, the reverse reaction takes exactly that quantity in.

concepts.term: Hydrated and anhydrous copper sulfate: a worked example of energy transfer
concepts.def: hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water, or CuSO4.5H2O ⇌ CuSO4 + 5H2O. Heating the blue hydrated solid to drive off water is endothermic and leaves a white solid; adding water to the white anhydrous solid is exothermic, the mixture warms up and the blue colour returns.

Apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products. Equilibrium can only be reached in such apparatus, because a substance that escapes is no longer available to take part in the reverse reaction.

The state reached, in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. Because the two rates are equal, the amounts of the substances present stop changing.
Equilibrium is dynamic, not static. Both reactions are still occurring at equilibrium; they are simply occurring at exactly the same rate as each other, so no change can be observed from outside.

The relative amounts of all the reactants and products present at equilibrium. These relative amounts depend on the conditions of the reaction, so the same reaction can settle with mostly products under one set of conditions and mostly reactants under another.

If a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, the system responds to counteract the change. The response opposes the change made; it reduces its effect but does not undo it entirely.

The principle that the effects of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium can be predicted from the idea that the system responds to counteract the change made. It is used to predict the direction in which the position of equilibrium moves, not how quickly equilibrium is reached.

Using given information about a reaction, such as its equation and whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, to say which way the position of equilibrium moves and whether the amount of a named substance rises or falls. Only this qualitative judgement is required.

concepts.term: Effect of a change in concentration
concepts.def: If the concentration of one of the reactants or products is changed, the system is no longer at equilibrium, and the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again. A change made to one substance therefore affects every substance in the equilibrium.

concepts.term: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
concepts.def: If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again. The system counteracts the extra reactant by using some of it up.

concepts.term: Decreasing the concentration of a product
concepts.def: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again. Removing a product does not stop the reaction; it causes more of the product to be made.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is increased, the relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction and decreases for an exothermic reaction.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is decreased, the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction and increases for an exothermic reaction.

concepts.term: Counting molecules from the symbol equation
concepts.def: For gaseous reactions, the number of molecules on each side is read from the balanced symbol equation, using the big numbers in front of the formulae. In N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 there are four molecules on the left and two on the right.

For gaseous reactions at equilibrium, an increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.

For gaseous reactions at equilibrium, a decrease in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the larger number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.

concepts.term: Equal numbers of molecules on each side
concepts.def: If the symbol equation shows the same number of gas molecules on both sides, as in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, a change in pressure gives no side for the equilibrium to shift towards, so the relative amounts at equilibrium are unaffected by pressure.

Data such as the percentage yield of a product measured at different temperatures, pressures or concentrations can be read backwards: the direction in which the yield moves tells you which way the position of equilibrium has shifted, and therefore what the reaction must be like.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes what makes a reaction a reversible reaction?
options: The reaction runs fully forwards and then runs fully backwards again
The products of the reaction can react to make the original reactants
The reaction ends with equal amounts of reactants and products
The reaction can be made to go faster or slower by adding a catalyst
mcqs.explain: This is the definition given in the specification: in some chemical reactions the products can react to produce the original reactants.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction is represented as A + B ⇌ C + D. What does this representation tell you about C and D?
options: They are products of the equation and so can never act as reactants
They are formed completely first and then break down to give A and B
They must always be present in the same amounts as A and B are
They can react together to form A and B again under the right conditions
mcqs.explain: The ⇌ symbol shows that the change works in both directions, so C and D can react to give the original reactants.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction is currently going in the forward direction. How could it be made to go in the reverse direction?
options: By changing the conditions, for example by cooling it instead of heating
It cannot be changed once the forward reaction has already started off
By waiting, because a reversible reaction turns round by itself at the end
By adding a catalyst, which drives the reaction the opposite way round
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions.

mcqs.q: Ammonium chloride is heated at the bottom of a test tube: NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. A white solid forms on the cool upper part of the tube. Why?
options: The solid melted, travelled up the tube as a vapour and then set again
The cooler conditions let ammonia and hydrogen chloride react together again
The forward reaction has now finished, so the reverse reaction can begin
Some ammonium chloride powder was carried up the tube by the hot gases
mcqs.explain: The reverse reaction is favoured by the cooler conditions higher up the tube, re-forming solid ammonium chloride.

mcqs.q: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. What can be said about the reverse reaction?
options: It is exothermic too, because reactions release energy
It is endothermic, but transfers less energy than the forward
It is exothermic, unless the conditions are changed first
It is endothermic, and transfers the same amount of energy
mcqs.explain: If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction it is endothermic in the other, with the same energy transfer.

mcqs.q: In a reversible reaction the forward reaction transfers 176 kJ of energy to the surroundings. What happens in the reverse reaction?
options: 176 kJ is taken in from the surroundings
Less than 176 kJ is taken in from them
176 kJ is given out to the surroundings
Twice as much, 352 kJ, is taken in
mcqs.explain: The same amount of energy is transferred in each case, but in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: Blue hydrated copper sulfate is heated and turns into white anhydrous copper sulfate and water. This change is endothermic. What happens when water is added to the white solid?
options: It turns blue and the mixture warms up, as energy is released
It turns blue and the mixture cools down, as energy is taken in
It stays white, because this change cannot be reversed again
It turns blue but no energy at all is transferred either way
mcqs.explain: The reverse of an endothermic change is exothermic, so the same amount of energy is transferred out.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction in a sealed flask has reached equilibrium. What is happening in the flask?
options: Both the forward and the reverse reactions have stopped happening
Equal amounts of both reactants and products are now present in it
The forward reaction is still going but the reverse one has stopped
The forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of the point at which equilibrium is reached.

mcqs.q: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products if equilibrium is to be reached?
options: It makes no real difference; equilibrium is reached in any container eventually
Both of the reactions stop as soon as any substance escapes from the flask
A substance that escapes cannot react back, so the rates never become equal
Escaping gas would cool the mixture down and slow both of the reactions
mcqs.explain: Equilibrium requires the reverse reaction to match the forward one, which needs the products to stay in the apparatus.

mcqs.q: A mixture at equilibrium in a sealed flask is left for a further hour with the conditions unchanged. What happens during that hour?
options: Nothing appears to change, because both of the reactions have stopped
The amounts slowly become equal to each other as the mixture stands
Nothing appears to change, but both reactions continue at equal rates
The forward reaction carries on slowly until the reactants are used up
mcqs.explain: Equilibrium is dynamic: the two reactions replace exactly what each other removes.

mcqs.q: What determines the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium?
options: The big numbers in the balanced symbol equation
The conditions the reaction is carried out under
Nothing, since the amounts are always equal there
The order in which the substances were mixed
mcqs.explain: The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.

mcqs.q: A system at equilibrium has one of its conditions changed. How does the system respond?
options: It cancels the change so that nothing is different at all
It stops reacting until the original conditions come back
It shifts in the direction that counteracts the change made
It shifts in the direction that increases the change made
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the system responds to counteract the change.

mcqs.q: Le Chatelier’s Principle is used to make predictions about systems at equilibrium. What does it allow you to predict?
options: How much faster a reaction goes when one of the conditions is changed
How long a reversible reaction takes to reach equilibrium in the first place
Exactly what mass of each product will be present once equilibrium is reached
Which way the position of equilibrium moves when a condition is changed
mcqs.explain: The principle predicts the effects of changing conditions on the relative amounts present at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: In the equilibrium 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 the forward reaction is exothermic. The mixture is cooled. Using Le Chatelier’s Principle, what is the effect?
options: The equilibrium shifts towards N2O4, so more N2O4 is present
The equilibrium shifts towards NO2, so more NO2 is present
The reaction slows down but the amounts present stay the same
The equilibrium shifts towards N2O4 only if pressure is raised
mcqs.explain: Cooling is counteracted by the direction that releases energy, which here is the forward reaction.

mcqs.q: Extra A is added to a system at equilibrium: A + B ⇌ C + D. Which concentrations change before equilibrium is reached again?
options: Only the concentration of A changes, because A was added
Only the concentrations of C and D change, and not A and B
The concentrations of all four of the substances change
No concentrations change, as the system is at equilibrium
mcqs.explain: The system is no longer at equilibrium, so the concentrations of all the substances change until it is reached again.

mcqs.q: In the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D, the concentration of B is increased. What happens next?
options: More C and D are formed until equilibrium is reached again
More A and B are formed, as that side has more in it now
The extra B is used up entirely and nothing else changes
Both reactions speed up but the amounts present are the same
mcqs.explain: If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.

mcqs.q: Product C is continuously removed from the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D. What is the effect on the system?
options: The reaction stops, because C is needed for it to continue
The equilibrium moves towards A and B, so less C is made
More A and B react together, so more C and D are formed
The amount of D falls as well, to match the fall in C
mcqs.explain: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.

mcqs.q: For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI at equilibrium, extra H2 is added. When equilibrium is reached again, the concentration of HI is higher and that of I2 is lower. What does this show?
options: Increasing a reactant caused more reactant to be formed
Adding H2 changed the concentration of H2 and nothing else
Adding H2 must have raised the temperature of the flask
Increasing a reactant caused more product to be formed
mcqs.explain: The data show HI rising and I2 falling, which is the forward reaction running further.

mcqs.q: The forward reaction of N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 is endothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased. What happens to the amount of NO2?
options: It increases, because a temperature rise favours the endothermic reaction
It decreases, because a temperature rise favours the exothermic reaction
It stays the same, because temperature changes only affect the rates
It increases at first and then returns to its original value again
mcqs.explain: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction when temperature is raised.

mcqs.q: The forward reaction of 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 is exothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased. What happens to the relative amount of SO3?
options: It increases, because a higher temperature always gives more product
It decreases, because the endothermic reverse reaction is favoured
It increases, because heating favours the exothermic forward change
It stays the same, because both sides of the equation contain oxygen
mcqs.explain: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an exothermic reaction when temperature is raised.

mcqs.q: The forward reaction of H2 + CO2 ⇌ CO + H2O is endothermic. The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is decreased. What happens to the amount of CO?
options: It decreases, because cooling favours the exothermic reverse reaction
It increases, because cooling favours the endothermic forward reaction
It stays the same, because cooling only slows the two reactions down
It decreases, because cooling stops the forward reaction completely
mcqs.explain: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction when temperature is lowered.

mcqs.q: The forward reaction of 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 is exothermic. The flask is placed in iced water. What happens to the relative amount of N2O4?
options: It decreases, because cooling favours the endothermic reverse reaction
It increases, because cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction
It decreases, because cooling always reduces the yield of a product
It increases, but only if the flask is squeezed to a smaller volume
mcqs.explain: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an exothermic reaction when temperature is lowered.

mcqs.q: The percentage yield of product Z at equilibrium is 68% at 200 °C, 45% at 300 °C and 27% at 400 °C. What does this show about the forward reaction?
options: It is endothermic, since raising the temperature lowers the yield
It is exothermic, since raising the temperature speeds it up more
It is exothermic, since raising the temperature lowers the yield
Nothing can be concluded without knowing the pressure that was used
mcqs.explain: A falling yield with rising temperature is what the specification states happens for an exothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: In the gaseous equilibrium N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?
options: Towards N2 and H2, the side with the larger number of them
Towards NH3, the side with the smaller number of molecules
Neither way, as the number of atoms is the same on each side
Towards NH3, but only if the temperature is raised as well
mcqs.explain: An increase in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules.

mcqs.q: In the gaseous equilibrium N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 the pressure is decreased. What is the effect on the equilibrium position?
options: It shifts towards N2O4, the side with the smaller number of molecules
It does not shift, but the yield of NO2 falls as the pressure falls
It shifts towards NO2, but only if the mixture is also heated up
It shifts towards NO2, the side with the larger number of molecules
mcqs.explain: A decrease in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the larger number of molecules.

mcqs.q: All the substances in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI are gases. The yield of HI at equilibrium is the same at 1 atm, 10 atm and 50 atm. Why does pressure have no effect here?
options: Raising the pressure should raise the yield, so the data are wrong
The equation has the same number of atoms on each side of it
Hydrogen and iodine are both made of molecules containing two atoms
The symbol equation shows two molecules on each side of it
mcqs.explain: With equal numbers of molecules on both sides there is no side with fewer molecules to shift towards.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.6.2 Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
